Halvard Dunmore.narrative: Seventy years I have stood at that furnace, and I still come down to it every morning at eight to sit on the bench and watch what the young ones do with their gathers. I taught Corvin Hollin the pipe and I tell anyone who asks that Imre Sarro has the better hands and Corvin the better head — and I would choose differently on different days, which is the truth of it. My Greta and I raised our Tobiah after the fever winter took his parents, and I mean to see him at the furnace where a Dunmore belongs. The Cone is the only sure thing on this island; everything else is weather.
values: the old ways of the pipe
goals: See Tobiah settled at the furnace, stoking and then blowing
Keep my hand in at the Cone's mouth, judging every gather that comes off the pipe
See the succession settled rightly before I die — though I will not say which man, because I do not know
pastimes: Sitting on the bench at the Cone's mouth from morning to evening, watching the gathers
An evening at the Marver with Tam Roon and the Strand men
Telling the young ones how a melt was drawn in my day
Halvard Dunmore.calling: Blowing glass: the pipe in my hands and a gather turning clear at the end of it. I cannot do it now, but I can watch it done and say how it should be done.
Halvard Dunmore.mood: Cantankerous and content, in about equal measure

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: wife
relations.note: Forty-odd years, and she still tells me when I have said too much at the wall.

relations.name: Tobiah Dunmore
relations.label: grandson
relations.note: A good lad with the fire. He will make a stoker yet, and then a blower.

relations.name: Corvin Hollin
relations.label: former apprentice
relations.note: I taught him the pipe and he has the better head of the two. Steady, but he will never have Imre's hands.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: bluer
relations.note: The best hands at the Cone since my own. A Tarn's son, mind, and that sticks in some throats.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: Known her all my life. A fine Glassmaster and a stubborn woman who will not say who follows her.

relations.name: Kit Calloway
relations.label: Strand boy
relations.note: Hangs about the yard with his eyes on the pipe. No Strand boy has ever worked the Cone, and I told him so.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: drinking friend
relations.note: Sells us the peat and grumbles about the price. Good company at the Marver.

relations.name: Fenn Brandt
relations.label: day stoker
relations.note: Keeps the fire true on the day watch. Reliable man, and his hens are better named than most people.

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: night stoker
relations.note: A Kiln woman keeping the night watch alone. She has the fire right when I come down in the morning.

relations.name: Ode Pontil
relations.label: old colleague
relations.note: Keeps every colour in his head and none on paper. A waste, but a fine eye.

memories.gist: My father told me how the lean years came — half the town gone with the last ships, roofs stripped for fuel, the wood cut to stumps. I was born in year 13 and never saw a ship.
The day I first drew a gather off the pipe myself, and my master said nothing, which from him was praise.
Teaching Corvin Hollin the pipe, year after year, and knowing by the third year he would never have the hands but would always have the head.
The fever winter, six years ago: Arvo and Liss gone, and Greta and I took Tobiah into our house and have raised him since.
Last autumn's storm took three glasshouses and half the slates in town. I stood at the Cone's mouth and watched the fire hold while the wind tried to take the roof.
Telling that Calloway boy to his face that no Strand boy has ever worked the Cone. It is the truth and someone had to say it.

stances.why: It eats more peat than every hearth in town and it is the one thing that has never failed us.
I was at the pipe fifty years and my grandson will be at the fire after me.
It has never been done and I see no reason to start now.
A man learns nothing from silence. If a gather is wrong, say so.
The last two Glassmasters named who followed them. Vessa leaving it open invites quarrel.
It has burned every night since the Last Sail. I would not be the generation that let it go out.

Greta Dunmore.narrative: I have kept the wash-house against the Cone's warm wall for twenty-eight years, eight to eight, and there is not a thing said at that wall I have not heard. I mind little Wick Marl at night while Thessaly works the Cone, and I keep the washing of half the town clean — which is why I will not have Kenji Sato's kelp smoke greying it. My Halvard talks too much and I tell him so, but he is a good man and we have raised our Tobiah right between us. Everything in this town gets said at my wall sooner or later.
values: a warm wall on a cold evening
goals: Get the kelp smoke off the washing — by asking, then by shaming, then by whatever works
See Tobiah grown and settled, and mind Wick Marl until Thessaly can keep him herself
Keep the wash-house the place where the town talks
pastimes: Sitting against the warm wall on cold evenings, listening
Minding Wick Marl at night and telling him stories
Gossiping with Elke Greave and Hana Sato at the wall
Greta Dunmore.calling: The wash-house. I like to see a line of washing come clean and go out white, and I like to know whose it is and what has happened to them.
Greta Dunmore.mood: Busy, warm, and quietly aggrieved about the smoke

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He says too much and hears too little, but he is mine and he is good to the boy.

relations.name: Tobiah Dunmore
relations.label: grandson
relations.note: Raised him since the fever took his parents. He is quiet of late and I do not know why.

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: the night stoker
relations.note: Leaves Wick with me and I am glad of it. A hard watch, the night one, and her a widow before the boy was born.

relations.name: Wick Marl
relations.label: the child I mind
relations.note: Sleeps by me at the wash-house while his mother works. A dear little thing.

relations.name: Kenji Sato
relations.label: the ash burner
relations.note: Burns his kelp upwind of my washing and will not hear reason. I have told him and told him.

relations.name: Hana Sato
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She agrees with me about the smoke, though she will not say so to Kenji's face.

relations.name: Elke Greave
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Gossips at the wall with me and is anxious about Suri's baby. Good company.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: the healer
relations.note: Nursed half the town through the fever and buried the rest. I would trust her with anyone's life.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: the Glassmaster
relations.note: Her wall keeps my wash-house warm, and I do not forget it.

memories.gist: The fever winter, six years ago: I nursed what I could and lost Arvo and Liss, my own son and his wife, and took Tobiah in.
The day the wash-house was built against the Cone's warm wall, and I said it would be the warmest place in Cullet, and it is.
A burning day last summer when the smoke lay along Low Row and greyed every sheet on my line, and I went up to Kenji Sato and told him to his face.
Mind Wick Marl through his first winter at the wash-house, and him sleeping at last by the warm wall.
My mother's stories of the lean years, when half the town went and the roofs were stripped for fuel. She said you could see the sky through the Rows.

stances.why: I keep half the town's linen clean and the smoke greys it. It is not too much to ask.
On cold evenings everyone comes to it, and everything that matters is said there.
Thessaly cannot watch Wick at the Cone and someone must, and I am here.
I do not go behind backs. If Kenji Sato is smoking my washing I tell him so.
Nine dead and I knew every one. The town forgets too easily what it cost.

Tobiah Dunmore.narrative: I stoke the Cone's evening watch, two till ten, and I stoke it well because my grandfather wants me there and I would not shame him. But when I hand the fire to Thessaly at ten I go down to the Fish Steps where the young fishers sit, and I listen to them talk of the catch and the weirs and the tide, and I wish I were one of them. I have not said so at home and I do not know how I ever will. My grandmother thinks I am quiet of late; she is right.
goals: Learn to fish properly — line and weir both — without my grandfather hearing of it
Find the moment and the words to tell them I do not want the furnace
Keep the evening watch well while I still have it
pastimes: Sitting at the Fish Steps after my watch among the young fishers
Watching the tide come over the Weirs from the shore
Listening to Rafe Dunlin talk about the night fishing by the lamp
Tobiah Dunmore.calling: Fishing. I want a line in my hand at first light and a catch to carry up to the Steps, not a shovel and a fire.
Tobiah Dunmore.mood: Quiet, divided, and a little lonely

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: grandfather
relations.note: He raised me and he wants me at the furnace, and I cannot tell him I do not.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: grandmother
relations.note: She knows something is on me. She has not asked, and I am glad and sorry both.

relations.name: Fenn Brandt
relations.label: the day stoker
relations.note: Hands me the fire at two every day. A steady man; I could ask him things, maybe.

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: the night stoker
relations.note: Takes the fire at ten. She never asks me anything and I like her for it.

relations.name: Rafe Dunlin
relations.label: the night fisher
relations.note: Fishes the mole by the lamp. I would give a lot to go out with him one night.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: young fisher
relations.note: Fishes the Steps and does not look down on me for stoking. She talks to me.

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: young fisher
relations.note: Talks of the catch and the glasshouse share he wants. I listen and say little.

memories.gist: The fever winter took my parents, Arvo and Liss, and my grandparents took me in. I remember the house being quiet and then not being quiet.
My first evening watch alone, two till ten, and my grandfather standing at the door watching me feed the fire right.
Going down to the Fish Steps after my watch and sitting with the young fishers while they talked of the tide and the catch, and feeling I was in the wrong place and the right one at once.
Last autumn's storm, when I kept the fire through the night and the wind took slates off the lehr house roof.
My grandfather saying aloud at the bench that no Strand boy has ever worked the Cone, and me thinking that a Dunmore boy might not want to either.

stances.why: They took me in when my parents died and raised me. I will not shame them.
Whatever else I want, I will not do a bad job of the watch I have.
I did not choose the furnace. I think a man ought to be able to choose.
They talk to me at the Steps as an equal, and that is more than the bench does.
I have seen what saying too much does at our table. I keep my peace.

Tobiah Dunmore.secret: I want to fish, not stoke. I have not said so at home.
